items.topic: Proto file organization: flat v1/ vs subdirectory structure
items.context: Agent-manager uses a subdirectory structure (v1/api/, v1/domain/) because it has separate API service definitions and domain types. The vrooli-events schemas are simpler — 3 files with no service definitions. However, if future protos are expected (e.g., admin API service definitions), a subdirectory now avoids a breaking reorganization later.

options.label: Flat v1/ directory
options.rationale: Simplest structure for 3 files. Matches the current scope. No premature hierarchy. Recommended because there are no service definitions and all 3 files share the same package — subdirectories add no organizational value here.

options.label: Subdirectories (v1/domain/, v1/api/)
options.rationale: Mirrors agent-manager pattern. Would separate domain types from future API service definitions. Adds complexity that isn't needed yet.

items.topic: PolicySnapshot content: embed full typed rule messages or use a generic wrapper
items.context: The PolicySnapshot message pushes the full ruleset to clients via SSE. Two approaches: (1) include typed repeated fields for each rule kind (repeated AccessRule, repeated RateLimit, repeated CircuitBreaker), or (2) use a single repeated PolicyRule wrapper with a oneof for the rule body. The typed approach is simpler and directly matches how clients will consume rules, but adding a new policy kind requires a schema change to PolicySnapshot. The wrapper approach is more extensible but adds indirection.

options.label: Typed repeated fields per rule kind
options.rationale: Direct: clients iterate `snapshot.access_rules`, `snapshot.rate_limits`, etc. No wrapper indirection. Adding a new kind requires a proto change, but the research conclusion says 'new policy kinds require proto schema changes, which is acceptable given the deliberate pace of policy evolution.' Recommended for simplicity.

options.label: PolicyRule wrapper with oneof body
options.rationale: Single `repeated PolicyRule rules` field where PolicyRule has a oneof {AccessRule, RateLimit, CircuitBreaker}. More extensible but clients must switch on the oneof to process rules. Adds complexity without clear near-term benefit.

items.topic: SubscriptionRequest: glob pattern string vs structured filter message
items.context: Clients subscribe to events via SSE. The research settled on glob patterns for event type matching (e.g., 'swarm-manager.backlog.*'). The question is whether SubscriptionRequest uses a simple string field for the glob, or a structured filter message that could also filter by source_scenario, target_scenario, etc.

options.label: Simple event_type_pattern string only
options.rationale: Matches research spec exactly. Minimalist — clients filter by event type glob. Additional filtering (source/target) can be added as new fields later without breaking the schema.

options.label: Structured filter with event_type_pattern + optional source/target patterns
options.rationale: More expressive from day one. Avoids needing a proto change when clients inevitably want to filter by source or target scenario. Fields: event_type_pattern (string), source_scenario_pattern (optional string), target_scenario_pattern (optional string). Recommended because the use case is obvious and the cost is minimal.

items.topic: AccessRule specificity: explicit score fields vs computed at evaluation time
items.context: The research specifies 'specificity scoring fields for segment-count evaluation' in AccessRule. This could mean: (1) store the computed specificity score as a field in the proto (pre-computed when the rule is created/updated), or (2) only store the pattern fields and compute specificity at evaluation time from the patterns. Option 1 avoids recomputation on every evaluation but requires the score to be maintained when rules change. Option 2 is simpler in the proto but means evaluation logic must compute scores.

options.label: Include a specificity_score int32 field (pre-computed)
options.rationale: Matches the description's mention of 'specificity scoring fields.' The score is stored when the rule is created/updated. Evaluation just compares pre-computed scores. Recommended because the scoring algorithm is deterministic and cheap to compute at write time, saving repeated computation at read time.

options.label: Omit score field, compute from patterns at evaluation time
options.rationale: Simpler proto — fewer fields to maintain. Score computation is trivial (count segments, classify each). Risk: if the scoring algorithm changes, stored scores become stale vs. computed scores are always fresh.
